text: This bell tower started leaning before it was even finished, and it's still standing centuries later. The reason lies in the ground beneath it. Work on the Tower of Pisa began in 1173. Five years later, as builders reached the second floor, it began to sink on one side. The problem was a foundation just three meters deep, set in soft, unstable soil. Then war stepped in. Pisa kept fighting its neighbors, and construction stopped for the better part of a century. That pause let the soil settle, and without it, the tower would almost certainly have toppled. When work resumed, builders tried to correct the tilt by making the upper floors shorter on one side. That's why the tower isn't just leaning, it's curved. It was finished in 1372, but the lean kept growing. By 1990 it had reached five and a half degrees, and the tower was closed to the public. Engineers cinched cables around the third level to hold it, then tried something gentle. Instead of pushing the tower, they coaxed the ground: they drilled angled holes under the raised north side and drew out small amounts of soil. That side settled a little, and the tower slowly eased back. By 2001 the tilt was just under four degrees. The tower reopened, and engineers expect it to stay secure for at least two hundred years. And that same soft soil helps it ride out earthquakes. The ground that nearly toppled the tower is the ground that saved it.
